lesson.title: Patterns in Mathematics
lesson.subtitle: Original concept guide · Class 6 Mathematics
learningGoals: Describe a number pattern using a clear rule.
Recognise counting, odd, even, square, triangular and cube number sequences.
Find missing terms without guessing randomly.
Explain why a pattern continues, rather than only stating the next number.
Connect number patterns to visual arrangements and shapes.

concepts.title: What is a mathematical pattern?
concepts.explanation: A pattern is an arrangement that follows a rule. The rule may describe how numbers change, how shapes repeat, or how objects are arranged. A good explanation states the rule clearly enough that another person can use it to continue the pattern.
concepts.example: In 4, 7, 10, 13, … each term is 3 more than the previous term. The rule is ‘add 3 each time’. The next term is 16.

concepts.title: Counting numbers
concepts.explanation: The counting numbers begin 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, … . Each term is one greater than the term before it.

concepts.title: Odd and even numbers
concepts.explanation: Positive even numbers are divisible by 2 without a remainder: 2, 4, 6, 8, … . Odd numbers are not divisible by 2 without a remainder: 1, 3, 5, 7, … . In both sequences shown, consecutive terms differ by 2.
concepts.example: The next two odd numbers after 17 are 19 and 21. The next two even numbers after 18 are 20 and 22.

concepts.title: Square numbers
concepts.explanation: A square number is the product of a whole number multiplied by itself. The first terms are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, … because 1² = 1, 2² = 4, 3² = 9, and so on.

concepts.title: Triangular numbers
concepts.explanation: Triangular numbers count dots arranged in rows of 1, then 2, then 3, and so on. Adding the first n counting numbers gives the nth triangular number: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, … . The differences are 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, … .
concepts.example: After 10, add 5 to get 15; then add 6 to get 21.

concepts.title: Cube numbers
concepts.explanation: A cube number is obtained by multiplying a whole number by itself three times. The sequence begins 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, … because 1³ = 1, 2³ = 8, 3³ = 27, and so on.

concepts.title: How to find a rule
concepts.explanation: Compare neighbouring terms. Check whether the same number is added or subtracted, whether terms are multiplied, or whether the sequence relates to squares, cubes or another known pattern. Test your proposed rule on more than one pair of terms.
concepts.example: In 5, 10, 20, 40, … each term is multiplied by 2. The next term is 80. Adding 5 would not fit all the changes, so it is not the rule.

concepts.title: Visual patterns
concepts.explanation: A drawing can reveal a rule that is hard to notice in a list of numbers. For example, square numbers can be represented by dots in an n-by-n square. Adding the next odd number creates the next larger square-shaped arrangement.
concepts.example: A 2 × 2 square has 4 dots. To form a 3 × 3 square with 9 dots, 5 more dots are needed. The increase from 4 to 9 is 5.

concepts.title: Virahanka-type sequence
concepts.explanation: In a Virahanka-type sequence, each new term is formed by adding the two terms immediately before it. Starting with 1, 2 gives 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, … . Always identify the starting terms before continuing the sequence.
concepts.example: After 8 and 13, add them: 8 + 13 = 21. The next term is 13 + 21 = 34.

concepts.title: Powers of 2 and powers of 3
concepts.explanation: A power sequence is formed by repeatedly multiplying by the same base. Powers of 2 begin 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, … . Powers of 3 begin 1, 3, 9, 27, 81, … . These are multiplicative patterns, not patterns formed by adding a fixed amount.
concepts.example: In 1, 3, 9, 27, … multiply by 3 each time, so the next term is 81.

concepts.title: Adding consecutive odd numbers
concepts.explanation: The first n positive odd numbers add to n². The first few cases are 1 = 1², 1 + 3 = 4 = 2², and 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 = 3². One way to understand this is to imagine adding an L-shaped border of new dots to grow one square into the next square.

concepts.title: Adding consecutive triangular numbers
concepts.explanation: Two consecutive triangular numbers can combine to make a square number. For example, 3 + 6 = 9 and 6 + 10 = 16. A dot diagram can show how two triangular arrangements fit together into a square.
concepts.example: The triangular numbers 10 and 15 add to 25, which is 5².

concepts.title: Patterns in shapes
concepts.explanation: Shape patterns can be described by counting sides, corners, edges or smaller repeated pieces. Regular polygons progress from a triangle with 3 sides to a quadrilateral with 4, a pentagon with 5, and a hexagon with 6 sides. A complete graph connects every pair of distinct points, and the number of connections follows a growing pattern. Repeatedly adding smaller triangular pieces can also create self-similar shapes such as a snowflake pattern.
concepts.example: A regular polygon with 7 sides is called a heptagon. The side-count pattern continues 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, … .

workedExamples.question: Find the next three terms: 2, 5, 8, 11, …
steps: The rule is add 3 each time.

workedExamples.question: What is the 7th square number?
steps: The nth square number is n × n.
For the 7th square number, use n = 7.

workedExamples.question: Find the missing term: 1, 3, 6, 10, __, 21.
steps: The differences increase by 1, so the next difference is +5.
10 + 5 = 15; then 15 + 6 = 21, which matches the final term.

workedExamples.question: A sequence is 3, 9, 27, 81, … . What is the next term?
How many dots are in a 5 × 5 square arrangement?
Continue the Virahanka-type sequence: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, __, __.
steps: Each term is the sum of the two terms before it.

workedExamples.question: Find the sum 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9.
steps: There are five consecutive positive odd numbers, beginning with 1.
The sum of the first n odd numbers is n².
Here n = 5, so the sum is 5² = 25.

practice.question: Write the next three counting numbers after 36.
Write the next two odd numbers after 23.
practice.reason: Odd numbers in this sequence increase by 2.

practice.question: Describe the rule: 7, 14, 28, 56, … .
practice.answer: Multiply each term by 2; the next term is 112.
practice.reason: Each term is double the previous term.

practice.question: Is 36 both a square number and an even number? Explain.
practice.answer: Yes. 36 = 6 × 6, so it is a square number, and it is divisible by 2, so it is even.
practice.reason: A number can belong to more than one number pattern.

practice.question: A student says the next term after 2, 4, 8 is 16. Is that certain without a rule?
practice.answer: No. It is a likely continuation if the rule is ‘multiply by 2’, but a finite list alone can fit other rules. State and test the intended rule.
practice.reason: Mathematics requires explaining the rule, not only guessing a term.

practice.question: Continue: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, __, __.
practice.reason: Add the two preceding terms to get each new term.

practice.question: Write the first five positive powers of 2, starting with 1.
Calculate 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 and describe the pattern.
practice.reason: The sum of the first five positive odd numbers is the fifth square number.

practice.question: A regular polygon has 8 sides. What is it called?
practice.reason: Polygon names are linked to their number of sides.

mcqs.q: What is the next term in 6, 9, 12, 15, …?
Which sequence contains only odd numbers?
Which is the correct description of 2, 4, 6, 8, …?
mcqs.why: The difference between consecutive terms is 2.

mcqs.q: A 4 × 4 square array contains how many objects?
mcqs.why: There are 4 rows with 4 objects in each: 4 × 4 = 16.
The differences are +2, +3, +4, +5; next add 6 to get 21.

mcqs.q: What should you do when explaining a pattern?
mcqs.why: A reliable explanation states a rule that fits the observed terms.

revision: A pattern follows a rule; explain the rule clearly.
Odd and even sequences increase by 2 when listed in order.
Square numbers: n² = n × n; first terms 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, … .
Triangular numbers: add the next counting number; 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, … .
Cube numbers: n³ = n × n × n; first terms 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, … .
A visual arrangement can help explain why a numerical pattern works.
For any sequence, test the proposed rule against all given terms.
Virahanka-type sequence: each term is the sum of the two previous terms, e.g. 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, … .
Powers of a base multiply repeatedly: powers of 2 are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, … .
The sum of the first n positive odd numbers equals n².
Two consecutive triangular numbers can add to a square number.
Shape patterns can be studied by counting sides, points, edges or repeated pieces.
